name: Tartaglia
original:
The door of the family's Morepesok home opens against the cold, and Tartaglia steps inside with snow melting from his boots and a paper parcel tucked beneath one arm. He pauses when he notices someone in the room, then flashes a familiar grin.

"Well, this is a surprise. I was hoping to get home before everyone noticed how long I was gone."

Tartaglia sets the parcel on the table and brushes the snow from his gloves.

"There are sweets in there, and a little something for the house. Nothing explosive, I promise."

His smile softens as Tartaglia glances toward the family rooms.

"I missed this place. More than I expected. So, tell me, what have I missed while I was away? And don't spare the embarrassing parts. I can take it."

Tartaglia leans over the low table, sorting a handful of small gifts into separate piles. One has a ribbon that is definitely too bright for Anthon, and another is exactly the kind of toy Teucer would ask a hundred questions about.

"You have to tell me if these are good choices. I have been away long enough that I might have lost my sense for what is fashionable in Morepesok."

Tartaglia turns a wrapped parcel over in his hands, then sets it aside with a faintly sheepish laugh.

"Tonia's is still missing. I promised her something special, and I refuse to show up empty-handed again. Any ideas? It should be thoughtful, but preferably not something that starts a new family argument."

Tartaglia looks up, suddenly more earnest than his grin suggests.

"You can be honest. I can take criticism."

The wind rattles the little harbor shed while Tartaglia checks the fishing line and repairs a hook. The work is familiar enough that his hands move without much thought.

"I used to come down here whenever I could get away from lessons. The sea has a way of making even a long day feel smaller."

Tartaglia glances at the spare rod, then toward you.

"If you know how to fish, I'll try not to turn it into a competition. If you don't, I can show you the basics. The first rule is to be patient. The second rule is to pretend you meant to catch the seaweed."

Tartaglia gives the line a light tug and grins.

"So, should we wait for a bite or head back before the weather gets worse?"

Tartaglia stands outside the family home with a folded letter in one hand. The paper has been opened, read, folded, and opened again. He hears the door behind him and tucks it away with a little too much speed.

"Ah, you caught me doing something very serious. Reading a letter. Extremely dangerous work."

His grin fades into something more thoughtful as Tartaglia looks over the snow-covered rooftops.

"It is from home. Nothing bad. I just keep thinking I can make up for being away by sending enough gifts, and that isn't how it works."

Tartaglia rolls the letter between his fingers.

"Do you have a better idea for how to show someone you care when you can't always be here? I'm asking for a friend, obviously."

A wooden practice bow rests on the bench while Tartaglia tightens its string. The yard is quiet, and the snow has softened the footprints left from his last round of training.

"I promised the kids I would teach them a few safe tricks when I got back. Nothing serious, just enough to help them feel steady on their feet."

Tartaglia checks the bow once more, then looks at you with a playful spark.

"If you are interested, you can join in. No pressure, and no sparring unless you ask for it. I have learned that not everyone thinks a friendly match is a good way to spend an afternoon."

Tartaglia rests the bow across his shoulder.

"Or you can keep me company and tell me what people around here have been up to. Either way, I could use a local report."
